statement: Afghanistan’s mean annual temperature increased by about 1.8°C between the 1951-1980 and 1981-2010 climatic periods, with larger reported warming in the South than nationally.
compact_statement: Strong observed warming.
uncertainty: Reanalysis-based historical result; does not alone establish impacts.

statement: The SNC’s analysis of 95th-percentile precipitation found no noticeable increase in heavy precipitation during 1950-2010, despite reports of increasing flood impacts.
compact_statement: Flood impacts ≠ proven rainfall trend.

source_refs.locator: viewer P49, Fig. 13 and accompanying text. (UNFCCC1)

uncertainty: Flood risk also depends on snowmelt, drought-hardened soils, land/exposure and infrastructure; later trends may differ.

statement: Seven CORDEX regional models projected roughly +1.5°C warming by 2050 under RCP4.5 and about +3°C under RCP8.5 relative to a 1976-2005 baseline; near-term Central Highlands/Hindu Kush warming was 1.5-1.7°C versus 1.1-1.4°C in lowlands.
compact_statement: Mid-century warming across scenarios.
uncertainty: Older-generation scenarios/models; stated projection uncertainty about ±2°C.

statement: The SNC projected a 5-10% spring precipitation decline through 2050 in the North, Central Highlands and East, while projecting about a 10% winter increase in the Hindu Kush and no significant precipitation trend in the arid South.
compact_statement: Precipitation change is region/season specific.
ecological_level: North; Central Highlands; East; Hindu Kush; South
uncertainty: Source explicitly says precipitation-model uncertainty is higher.

statement: SIPRI/NUPI reports mean annual temperature rising from 12.23°C in 1960 to 14.24°C in 2024 and summarizes current models as projecting a further 1.5-3°C increase by 2050 depending on emissions.
compact_statement: Recent synthesis confirms warming direction.

source_refs.locator: PDF P1, “Climate exposure: trends and projections”. (NUPI3)

uncertainty: Secondary synthesis rather than primary climate dataset; scenario details abbreviated.

statement: Afghanistan’s 2015 NDC identified funding gaps, lack of expertise, inadequate historical climate data, weak public awareness and security as major adaptation barriers and estimated $10.785 billion for its listed adaptation actions over ten years.
compact_statement: Adaptation constrained by finance, data, expertise and security.

source_refs.locator: PDF P4, “Adaptation Needs and Means of Implementation,” lines 188-240. (UNFCCC5)

uncertainty: Government self-assessment from 2015; institutional arrangements subsequently changed substantially.

statement: In September-October 2025, IPC classified an estimated 13.8 million people, 28% of the analysed population, in IPC Phase 3 or worse, including about 2.9 million in Phase 4.
compact_statement: Acute food insecurity remained widespread.
uncertainty: IPC explicitly identifies several simultaneous drivers; not climate-attributable as a whole.

statement: IPC reported the 2025 drought as the most extensive since 2018 and 2021 and estimated 3.4 million people in 65 districts were severely affected through food, water and livelihood impacts.
compact_statement: 2025 drought had broad livelihood exposure.
ecological_level: 65 districts; especially cited Daikundi, Helmand, Kandahar
uncertainty: IPC is synthesizing FAO/OCHA estimates; the statistic does not establish anthropogenic attribution.

statement: IPC projected 13.8 million people in Phase 3 or worse for April-September 2026, including about 2.889 million in Phase 4.
compact_statement: Food insecurity projected to remain high in 2026.
uncertainty: Projection contingent on assumptions about weather, production, assistance, markets and borders.

statement: In WoAA 2025, 64% of households reported drought impacts, up from 34% in 2024; 92% did so in the Central Highlands. Flood exposure was 10%, while earthquake exposure was recorded separately at below 1% because fieldwork preceded later earthquakes.
compact_statement: Drought dominated 2025 reported environmental exposure.

source_refs.locator: viewer P40-P41, Fig. 45 and drought discussion. (UNDP2)

uncertainty: Household self-report; earthquake timing demonstrates why geological hazards must be kept distinct.

statement: The share of households reporting full drinking-water sufficiency fell from 59% in 2024 to 44% in 2025; Central Highlands and Eastern regions experienced the largest declines.
compact_statement: Drinking-water sufficiency worsened.
uncertainty: Report interprets drought, population pressure and infrastructure jointly; shares are survey responses.

statement: In UNDP’s 2025 12-province comparison, recent returnees had a 92% subsistence-insecurity headcount, versus 85% among non-recent returnees and 74% among local communities.
compact_statement: Recent returnees showed higher multidimensional deprivation.
uncertainty: Subsample finding, not automatically national for all returnees.

statement: Female-headed households in the common 2025 survey sample increasingly relied on home-based production; 68% of adults were working versus 54% in male-headed households, but child labour was 10% versus 7%, making this coping strategy potentially costly.
compact_statement: Home-based coping can carry human-capital costs.
uncertainty: Observational comparison; UNDP’s interpretation of adaptation mechanism is not causal proof.

statement: About 17% of surveyed women returnees in Herat, Nangarhar and Kabul were employed after return; 77% lacked tools for income generation and only 9% reported having needed equipment.
compact_statement: Women returnees face strong livelihood-capacity constraints.
uncertainty: Telephone/cross-sectional sample excludes some women without phone access; no causal inference.

statement: More than 75% of 292 surveyed returnee households in Herat and Kandahar said clean-water access was difficult or very difficult, and over 70% said it had worsened during the previous six months as returns increased.
compact_statement: Returns overlap with severe local water stress.

source_refs.locator: PDF P2/P7, methodology and Water Impacts. (Mercy Corps4)

uncertainty: “Due to returns” is respondent/report attribution; cannot quantify causal share versus drought, extraction and infrastructure.

statement: Mercy Corps respondents reported water-related community tensions roughly three times more often in urban than rural surveyed communities, and about 80% of reported cases were described as unresolved by community mediation.
compact_statement: Local water stress can become a social-tension mediator.
ecological_level: Surveyed urban/rural sites in Herat and Kandahar
geographies: Surveyed urban/rural sites in Herat and Kandahar

source_refs.locator: PDF P9, “Financial, Social and Protection Costs”. (Mercy Corps4)

uncertainty: Local perceptions; water stress itself reflects non-climate drivers. No evidence that these tensions caused organized violence.

statement: In three Balkh districts, participants described drought-related displacement as a gradual process in which depleted livelihoods, higher costs and reduced access to basic services accumulated until households could no longer cope.
compact_statement: Drought -> livelihood erosion -> displacement, locally documented.
uncertainty: Purposive qualitative study; process evidence is stronger than prevalence evidence and remains local.

statement: Balkh participants made 17 references to intracommunity tensions associated with varying combinations of local conflict dynamics, personal grievances and competition for scarce resources, but ten references indicated insecurity was not an issue.
compact_statement: Conflict evidence in Balkh is mixed, not deterministic.
uncertainty: Small purposive qualitative sample; divergent reports; no causal attribution to climate.

statement: Ten participants in the Balkh study said displaced households mainly relied on family, friends or the wider host community to meet basic needs or find work.
compact_statement: Informal solidarity is a resilience resource.
uncertainty: Very small qualitative evidence; availability and durability of support are not quantified.

statement: Balkh climate-affected IDPs reported coping measures including debt, asset sales, drinking unsafe water, family separation and reduced meals.
compact_statement: Coping often depletes future resilience.
uncertainty: Qualitative local findings; prevalence unknown.

statement: SIPRI/NUPI concludes that climate change is rarely the main driver of conflict in Afghanistan and organizes relevant mechanisms around livelihood impacts, migration/mobility, armed actors/security and political-economic grievances.
compact_statement: Climate-FCV effects are mediated.

source_refs.locator: PDF P1, “Climate-related peace and security risks”. (NUPI3)

uncertainty: Expert synthesis; does not estimate causal effects.

statement: SIPRI/NUPI finds that restrictions on women’s and girls’ rights and sociocultural norms increase dependence and constrain participation and disaster-assistance access, thereby reducing adaptive capacity.
compact_statement: Gender restrictions amplify climate vulnerability.
uncertainty: General synthesis; extent varies locally and by household.

statement: SIPRI/NUPI identifies governance challenges, political context and donor hesitancy as impediments to effective climate-adaptation strategies.
compact_statement: Political/institutional conditions constrain adaptation.
uncertainty: Expert synthesis; separate effects of sanctions, governance and donor choices are not quantified.

statement: SIPRI/NUPI describes shared-water tensions with Iran as arising from a combination of water stress, water-management decisions, dam/irrigation plans and political instability, while also identifying transboundary water cooperation as a possible entry point for dialogue.
compact_statement: Shared water can generate both tension and cooperation.
uncertainty: Climate contribution cannot be separated from allocation, infrastructure and political decisions; peace benefit is potential rather than evaluated outcome.

statement: UNDP reports humanitarian funding declining from $1.62 billion in 2024 to $0.91 billion in 2025, while more than 440 health facilities were closed or suspended because of funding shortages.
compact_statement: Aid contraction weakened service-delivery capacity.
uncertainty: Funding and service decline are not climate impacts; they can increase vulnerability to multiple shocks.

statement: Current World Bank/ARTF support keeps funds outside de facto-authority systems and control and uses independent third-party monitoring to verify project compliance.
compact_statement: External delivery architecture substitutes for normal state channels.
uncertainty: Demonstrates delivery arrangements, not effectiveness or adaptation outcomes.

statement: The 2023 CDRRP terminal evaluation rated overall project outcomes 5.25/6, but activities had been suspended in August 2021 and never resumed, and the evaluator lacked some information needed for cost-effectiveness assessment.
compact_statement: Positive project rating with major evaluation/context constraints.

source_refs.locator: PDF P1, P21 and P73, Exhibit 9-5. (Evaluation Resource Center6)

uncertainty: Terminal evaluation without counterfactual; almost two-year post-suspension gap; remote methodology.

statement: The 2019 CCAP terminal evaluation rated overall project results “Satisfactory” and judged that target rural livelihoods and exposure to climate-induced disaster risk had improved within the project areas.
compact_statement: Earlier adaptation project rated satisfactory.

source_refs.locator: PDF P10, evaluation rating table/conclusion. (Evaluation Resource Center11)

uncertainty: Evaluator judgement, not counterfactual impact estimate; cannot be generalized beyond project areas or to present institutions.

statement: The same 2019 evaluation rated M&E at entry and implementation only moderately satisfactory, found many indicators insufficiently SMART/outcome-focused, and noted the lack of an adequate exit strategy for some infrastructure.
compact_statement: Evaluation design and sustainability weaknesses limited confidence.

source_refs.locator: PDF P41-P43 §3.2.5 and P53 sustainability/exit discussion. (Evaluation Resource Center11)

uncertainty: Clear evaluation finding; actual long-term failure/success was not measured.

statement: The World Bank estimated nearly 3.7 million returns from Iran and Pakistan during Afghanistan’s FY2025, population growth of about 11% and a 5.6% fall in GDP per capita, with return concentrations adding pressure to health, nutrition and WASH services.
compact_statement: Mass returns are an independent vulnerability and service-pressure driver.
ecological_level: National; notably Herat in service discussion

source_refs.locator: viewer P7/P14 and P26. (The World Bank9)

uncertainty: Macro estimates; return effects interact with aid, markets, borders and drought but should not be labelled climate effects.
